title: Explain the 5 internal properties of an RDD — (1) list of partitions, (2) computation function per partition, (3) dependencies/lineage (narrow vs wide), (4) optional Partitioner (HashPartitioner / RangePartitioner), (5) preferred locations (data locality: PROCESS_LOCAL → NODE_LOCAL → RACK_LOCAL → ANY).
shortTitle: The five internal properties of an RDD

s1_definition.profdef: Every RDD is defined internally by five properties. First, a list of partitions, which are the chunks the data is split into. Second, a computation function that tells Spark how to compute each partition. Third, a list of dependencies on parent RDDs, which form the lineage and are either narrow or wide. Fourth, an optional Partitioner for key-value RDDs, such as a HashPartitioner or RangePartitioner, that controls how keys map to partitions. Fifth, an optional list of preferred locations per partition for data locality, which Spark uses to schedule tasks close to their data.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture the National Bank of India's archive of transaction records. The list of partitions is how the archive is divided into boxes. The computation function is the instruction slip on each box telling the clerk how to produce that box's contents. The dependencies are the chain of previous boxes a box was derived from, so you can rebuild it if lost. The Partitioner is the filing rule that decides which box a given account's records go into, so all of one account's records land together. And the preferred locations are notes saying "this box is already on the third floor, so send a clerk who is already there" instead of hauling it across the building.
s1_definition.oneliner: An RDD is fully described by its partitions, its per-partition compute function, its parent dependencies (lineage), an optional partitioner, and optional preferred locations for data locality.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Every RDD is defined internally by five properties. First, a list of partitions, which are the chunks the data is split into. Second, a computation function that tells Spark how to compute each partition. Third, a list of dependencies on parent RDDs, which form the lineage and are either narrow or wide. Fourth, an optional Partitioner for key-value RDDs, such as a HashPartitioner or RangePartitioner, that controls how keys map to partitions. Fifth, an optional list of preferred locations per partition for data locality, which Spark uses to schedule tasks close to their data.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture the National Bank of India's archive of transaction records. The list of partitions is how the archive is divided into boxes. The computation function is the instruction slip on each box telling the clerk how to produce that box's contents. The dependencies are the chain of previous boxes a box was derived from, so you can rebuild it if lost. The Partitioner is the filing rule that decides which box a given account's records go into, so all of one account's records land together. And the preferred locations are notes saying "this box is already on the third floor, so send a clerk who is already there" instead of hauling it across the building.

**One line to remember:** An RDD is fully described by its partitions, its per-partition compute function, its parent dependencies (lineage), an optional partitioner, and optional preferred locations for data locality.

sections.s2_technical:
The first property, the list of partitions, defines the unit of parallelism. Each partition becomes one task in a stage, so the number of partitions sets how many tasks run and therefore how much the cluster can do in parallel. You can see them through methods that report the partition count, and the right number balances parallelism against scheduling overhead.

The second property, the computation function per partition, is the function Spark applies to produce the records of a given partition. For a base RDD this reads from storage; for a derived RDD it applies the transformation to the parent's partition. This is what makes an RDD "describable" rather than "materialized" — it knows how to compute itself on demand.

The third property, dependencies, is the lineage, and it comes in two flavours. A narrow dependency means each parent partition is used by at most one child partition, as with map and filter, so no data moves across the network and Spark can pipeline these within one stage. A wide dependency means a single parent partition feeds many child partitions, as with groupByKey, reduceByKey, and join, which requires a shuffle that redistributes data across the cluster and creates a stage boundary. Knowing which operations are wide is the key to predicting where expensive shuffles happen.

The fourth property, the optional Partitioner, applies to key-value RDDs and controls how keys are assigned to partitions. A HashPartitioner sends a key to a partition based on the hash of the key, giving even distribution, while a RangePartitioner assigns contiguous key ranges to partitions, which helps sorting and range queries. A well-chosen partitioner can eliminate shuffles: if two RDDs share the same partitioner, a join between them can avoid moving data. The fifth property, preferred locations, lets each partition advertise where its data already lives so the scheduler can place the task there. Spark tries the best locality first — PROCESS_LOCAL, meaning the data is in the same executor's memory, then NODE_LOCAL on the same machine, then RACK_LOCAL in the same rack, then ANY. A senior nuance is that these five properties are exactly what you implement when you write a custom RDD, and together they explain almost every Spark performance question: partition count drives parallelism, dependencies drive shuffles and stages, the partitioner can remove shuffles, and preferred locations minimize network transfer. In banking workloads, partitioning transaction data by account id so an account's records stay together let us join and aggregate with far fewer shuffles.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The bank's transaction archive must be split so many clerks work in parallel. This is exactly the list of partitions.

Problem 2 — Each box needs an instruction for producing its contents, and derived boxes must know their source. This is exactly the compute function and the dependency lineage.

Problem 3 — All of one account's records should land in the same box to avoid shuffling during aggregation, and tasks should run near their data. This is exactly the Partitioner and preferred locations.

The mini-project models an RDD descriptor in Java. `RddDescriptor` exposes the five properties: a list of partitions, a compute function, a dependency list with a narrow/wide flag, an optional `HashPartitioner`, and preferred locations per partition. The demo builds a base descriptor over Rajesh's and Priya's transactions, derives a narrow (map) child and a wide (groupBy) child, applies a hash partitioner by account id, and prints the preferred locality for each partition.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three transactions in two partitions — partition 0 has Rajesh Rs.1000, partition 1 has Priya Rs.500 and Rajesh Rs.3000. Preferred locations say partition 0 is on worker-1 and partition 1 is on worker-2.

Step 1: The base descriptor is created with all five properties — two partitions, a compute function that returns a partition by index, an empty dependency list because it is a root, a HashPartitioner over two partitions, and the two preferred locations.

Step 2: We read property one (two partitions), property four (the HashPartitioner), and property five (partition 0 prefers worker-1). These describe the RDD without materializing anything beyond the base data.

Step 3: We derive a narrow child by mapping each transaction to its amount. Because map is narrow, each parent partition feeds exactly one child partition and no data crosses the network; the child's single dependency reports causesShuffle as false.

Step 4: We derive a wide child by repartitioning transactions by account id using a HashPartitioner. This moves records across partitions so that all of one account's transactions land together, which is a shuffle; the child's dependency reports causesShuffle as true.

Step 5: The logs confirm the two kinds of dependency and show that the wide operation is where Spark would insert a stage boundary. The data for the wide child now has Rajesh's two transactions grouped and Priya's one transaction grouped by the partitioner.

Step 6: The final state demonstrates all five properties working together: partitions set parallelism, the compute function produces each partition, dependencies distinguish narrow from wide, the partitioner controls key placement, and preferred locations guide scheduling.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Every RDD in Spark is defined internally by five properties, and I like to list them because they explain almost every performance question you can be asked. The first is the list of partitions, which are the chunks the data is divided into and which directly set the unit of parallelism, because Spark creates one task per partition. The second is the computation function per partition, which tells Spark how to produce the records of any given partition on demand, either by reading storage for a base RDD or by applying a transformation to the parent for a derived RDD. The third is the list of dependencies on parent RDDs, which forms the lineage.

Those dependencies come in two kinds, and this is the most important part for performance. A narrow dependency means each parent partition feeds at most one child partition, as with map and filter, so no data moves across the network and Spark pipelines them inside a single stage. A wide dependency means one parent partition feeds many children, as with groupByKey, reduceByKey, and join, which forces a shuffle that redistributes data across the cluster and creates a stage boundary. The fourth property is the optional Partitioner for key-value RDDs — a HashPartitioner for even distribution or a RangePartitioner for sorted ranges — and choosing it well can eliminate shuffles, because two RDDs sharing a partitioner can be joined without moving data. The fifth is the optional list of preferred locations, the data-locality hints Spark uses to schedule a task where its data already lives, trying PROCESS_LOCAL, then NODE_LOCAL, then RACK_LOCAL, then ANY.

In my project at the National Bank of India these five properties were my mental checklist whenever a job was slow. I tuned the partition count against executor cores for parallelism, I traced the dependency chain to find where expensive shuffles happened, and most impactfully I partitioned transaction data by account id so that an account's records stayed together, which let later joins and aggregations run with far fewer shuffles. Understanding that an RDD is nothing more than these five properties is what let me reason about and fix real performance problems rather than guessing.
